immutable

ih-MYOO-tuh-buhl -- from Latin in- ('not') + mutare ('to change'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Immutable is permanent or cannot be changed.

The old monk taught that certain moral truths were immutable, unaffected by fashion or the passing of centuries.

Example

No matter how many times the software is updated, the museum insists that the original architectural plans of the building itself remain immutable, never to be altered.

Immutable describes exactly that permanent, unchangeable quality -- something fixed no matter what else changes around it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unalterable: Unalterable makes the same hard claim as immutable -- incapable of being changed -- and the two are often interchangeable. The difference is register: unalterable is the plainer choice for contracts, deadlines, and decisions, while immutable is the formal, philosophical word reached for with laws of nature and moral truths.

irrevocable: Irrevocable describes a step already taken that no one can call back -- a signed surrender, a spent inheritance. Immutable describes a standing thing that cannot be altered at all, like a law of nature. An irrevocable decision was changeable right up until it was made; an immutable truth never was.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mutable: likely to change

volatile: liable to change rapidly and unpredictably

Where it sits · how firmly it resists change — fixed → immutable → eternal

fixed vs. immutable: Fixed is a milder, more everyday word -- a fixed schedule or fixed price can still technically be changed by someone with authority to do so, while immutable suggests something that cannot be changed under any circumstances.

eternal vs. immutable: Eternal pushes past immutable -- an immutable law cannot be changed, but an eternal one goes further still: it has always held and always will, standing outside time itself, with nothing before it and nothing after.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before m) (Latin)

Root — mut

Root — mut: to change (from Latin mutare)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be (Latin -abilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- ('not' -- the shape in- takes before m) + mut ('to change', from Latin mutare) + -able ('able to be') spell immutable: literally 'not changeable', fixed and permanent no matter what else shifts around it.

Use the root in a new word: mutate

Use the root in a new word: mutate: Certain viruses mutate so quickly that last year's treatment may no longer fully protect against this year's strain.

Word Choice

Immutable is a fairly formal, often philosophical or scientific word -- it's commonly paired with 'law,' 'truth,' or 'fact' to describe something treated as permanently fixed, beyond ordinary change.
